q01,multi,How long do eggs last in the fridge?,Fresh eggs in the shell: 3-5 weeks in the fridge (FDA storage chart); the FDA egg page says use them within 3 weeks for best quality.,"According to FDA guidance, fresh eggs in the shell should be stored promptly in a clean refrigerator at 40° F or below in their original carton and used within 3 weeks for best quality [fda:what-you-need-know-about-egg-safety
Storage times for other egg products in the refrigerator include:
* **Fresh, in shell:** 3 - 5 weeks [fda_storage_chart
* **Raw yolks, whites:** 2 - 4 days [fda_storage_chart
* **Hard cooked:** 1 week [fda_storage_chart
* **Liquid pasteurized eggs or egg substitutes:** 3 days if opened, or 10 days if unopened [fda_storage_chart
* **Leftover cooked egg dishes:** 3 to 4 days [fda:what-you-need-know-about-egg-safety

column1: q03,single,My pesto is past its date but I kept it frozen. Can I still eat it?,"Pesto is not listed, but the chart says food kept frozen at 0°F stays safe indefinitely; freezer times and dates are about quality, not safety.","Yes, you can still eat it. Product date labels (such as ""expires on,"" ""sell by,"" or ""best by"") indicate quality and flavor rather than safety [fda:how-cut-food-waste-and-maintain-food-safety]. Because freezing at 0° F (-18° C) keeps food safe indefinitely, the recommended freezer storage times are for quality only [fda_storage_chart

When you are ready to use the pesto, examine it for signs of spoilage and check if it has changed noticeably in color, consistency, or texture [fda:how-cut-food-waste-and-maintain-food-safety].","fda:how-cut-food-waste-and-maintain-food-safety

column1: q04,single,How long does chicken last if I freeze it?,"Raw chicken: whole 1 year, parts 9 months (quality; frozen food stays safe indefinitely).","According to FDA guidelines, because freezing at 0°F (-18°C) keeps food safe indefinitely, recommended freezer storage times are for quality rather than safety [fda_storage_chart
For chicken in the freezer:
* **Whole chicken or turkey:** 1 year [fda_storage_chart
* **Chicken or turkey parts:** 9 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Giblets:** 3–4 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Fried chicken:** 4 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Cooked poultry dishes:** 4–6 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Chicken pieces (plain):** 4 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Chicken pieces covered with broth or gravy:** 6 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Chicken nuggets and patties:** 1–3 months [fda_storage_chart

Additionally, if you are freezing meat and poultry in its original package for longer than 2 months, the FDA recommends overwrapping the package with airtight heavy-duty foil, plastic wrap, or freezer paper, or placing it inside a plastic bag [fda_storage_chart

column1: q05,single,How long does meat last if I freeze it?,"Raw beef/pork: steaks 6-12 months, chops 4-6 months, roasts 4-12 months; hamburger/ground meat 3-4 months.","Because freezing at 0°F (-18°C) keeps food safe indefinitely, the recommended freezer storage times are for quality only [fda_storage_chart
According to the FDA's Refrigerator & Freezer Storage Chart, recommended freezer times for quality include:
* **Fresh Meat (Beef, Veal, Lamb, & Pork):**
* Steaks: 6–12 months [fda_storage_chart
* Chops: 4–6 months [fda_storage_chart
* Roasts: 4–12 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Raw Hamburger, Ground & Stew Meat:**
* Hamburger & stew meats: 3–4 months [fda_storage_chart
* Ground turkey, veal, pork, lamb: 3–4 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Fresh Poultry:**
* Chicken or turkey, whole: 1 year [fda_storage_chart
* Chicken or turkey, parts: 9 months [fda_storage_chart
* Giblets: 3–4 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Bacon & Sausage:**
* Bacon: 1 month [fda_storage_chart
* Sausage, raw from pork, beef, chicken, or turkey: 1–2 months [fda_storage_chart
* Smoked breakfast links, patties: 1–2 months [fda_storage_chart
* **Meat Leftovers:**
* Cooked meat & meat dishes: 2–3 months [fda_storage_chart
* Gravy & meat broth: 2–3 months [fda_storage_chart

If you are freezing meat and poultry in its original package for longer than 2 months, overwrap these packages with airtight heavy-duty foil, plastic wrap, or freezer paper; or place the package inside a plastic bag [fda_storage_chart

column1: ### Types and Causes

* **Foodborne Botulism:** A severe type of food poisoning caused by ingesting foods containing the toxin produced by *C. botulinum*, most often developing after consumption of improperly processed and inadequately cooked home-preserved foods [bad_bug_book
* **Infant Botulism:** A serious illness caused by the ingestion of *C. botulinum* spores that colonize and produce toxin in the intestinal tracts of infants [bad_bug_book
column2: p. 108, Clostridium botulinum > 2. Disease (part 2)]. Honey is a known dietary reservoir of these spores and should never be fed to children under 1 year of age [bad_bug_book

### Symptoms

* **Adult / Foodborne Symptoms:** Early symptoms typically start 18 to 36 hours after ingesting food containing the toxin (though times can vary from 4 hours to 8 days) and include double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, dry mouth, and muscle weakness [bad_bug_book
